name: Avoiding ultra-processed foods

lead: This approach means cutting industrially manufactured, multi-ingredient foods and eating mostly whole or minimally processed ones. People use it to lose body fat and, in some circles, to improve skin.

Eating whole foods tends to mean fewer excess calories, which lowers body fat over time. Observational studies link high ultra-processed food intake with obesity and chronic disease, though critics say the category is poorly defined and randomised evidence is limited. Appearance trials of avoiding them have not been done.

paras: Users read ingredient lists, cook from basic ingredients and swap packaged snacks, sodas and ready meals for whole or minimally processed foods. Most combine it with a calorie target.
Little direct risk is reported. One study noted that avoiding UPFs could change nutrient intake, since fortified breads and cereals are often classed as UPFs.

angle.text: Swapping ultra-processed foods for whole foods trims excess calories, which lowers body fat and gives a leaner look; some also aim for clearer skin. Intake is linked to health outcomes in observational studies, and appearance trials have not been done.

lead: Avoiding ultra-processed foods (UPFs) is a whole-food eating approach in which people build meals from minimally processed ingredients such as fresh produce, eggs, meat, legumes and grains. In looks-focused circles it is used mainly as a way to stay lean, so that jawline and facial structure show, and to eat for clearer-looking skin and steady energy for training.[1][2]

The approach rests on the NOVA classification, proposed in 2009 by Carlos Monteiro and colleagues at the University of Sao Paulo, which groups foods by the degree and purpose of processing rather than by nutrients.[1][2] Group 4, the ultra-processed foods, are industrial formulations with many ingredients, often including additives and substances rarely used in home cooking, such as flavourings, emulsifiers and hydrogenated oils.[2] Examples include most industrially made bread, frozen pizza, instant noodles, flavoured yoghurt and most junk food.[1]

Observational studies associate higher UPF intake with obesity, cardiometabolic disease and earlier death, and several South American countries advise avoiding UPFs in their dietary guidelines.[1] Critics, including Arne Astrup, describe the category as loosely defined and note that the evidence is largely observational.[1]
infobox: Carlos Monteiro and colleagues, University of Sao Paulo, 2009[2]

paras: NOVA has four groups. Group 1 is unprocessed or minimally processed food such as fresh or frozen produce, grains, legumes, meat, eggs and milk. Group 2 is processed culinary ingredients such as oils, salt, sugar and butter. Group 3 is processed foods such as cheese, canned vegetables and simple breads. Group 4 is ultra-processed food.[2]

NOVA considers ingredients, processing and marketing, not nutrient content, and no universally accepted definition of UPF exists yet, including at Codex Alimentarius and EFSA.[1] The name comes from a 2010 article title and is not an acronym.[2] Monteiro's work grew out of observations in Brazil in the mid-1990s that obesity was rising among poorer households as processed products spread.[2]

Proponents link UPF avoidance to body composition: Wikipedia notes UPFs tend to be low in fibre and protein, high in energy density and high-glycaemic, features proposed to encourage overeating.[1] Someone aiming for a lean look may therefore swap them for whole foods. Wikipedia does not discuss skin or facial appearance in connection with UPFs.

Epidemiological studies associate UPF consumption with obesity and noncommunicable disease. A 2023 meta-analysis of 415,554 participants reported 12 percent higher type 2 diabetes risk per 10 percent increase in intake, a 2024 meta-analysis found 17 percent higher cardiovascular risk for the highest versus lowest consumers, and a 2025 meta-analysis found 15 percent higher all-cause mortality.[1] A 2024 BMJ umbrella review of 32 meta-analyses linked UPFs to adverse outcomes with possible heterogeneity between subgroups.[1]

Critics say the concept is poorly defined, that the evidence is observational, and that some processing is beneficial; a 2023 Lancet study found cereals and bread inversely associated with disease while animal-based products and sweetened drinks were most strongly associated.[1] The one frequently cited randomised trial did not control for macronutrient profile or energy density, and randomised trials have not confirmed the obesity link.[1] The UK Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition recommended more research rather than adopting a position.[1]
A 2022 study in Australia found that avoiding UPFs could alter nutrient intakes, since many fortified breads and cereals are classed as UPF yet are recommended core foods in national guidelines.[3]
No studies found testing UPF avoidance specifically for appearance outcomes such as skin or facial leanness. Observational and meta-analytic research on health outcomes is summarised above.[1][3]

timeline.event: Monteiro and colleagues propose the NOVA classification.[2]
Brazil's dietary guidelines draw on NOVA and advise avoiding ultra-processed products.[2]
Meta-analysis links UPF intake to higher type 2 diabetes risk.[1]
Meta-analysis reports higher all-cause mortality for the highest UPF consumers.[1]
